'''Muriel Nissel''' (née Griffiths; 30 January 1921 – 2010) was a British statistician and civil servant. Together with [[Claus Moser]], she created "a national survey analysing trends in social welfare", that was to become ''[[Social Trends]]'', first published in 1970, and considered to be the "statistician's bible", before working on the "distribution and [[redistribution of wealth]]". Nissel also wrote well-regarded books, including ''People Count &ndash; a history of the General Register Office'', and ''Married to the Amadeus: Life with a String Quartet''.

==Early life==
She was born Muriel Griffiths on 30 January 1921 at 38 Perham Road, [[Fulham]], London, the only child of Evan Griffiths, a civil servant who worked for the [[General Post Office]], and his wife, Bessie May Griffiths, née Phillips, a [[governess]].<ref name="ONDB">{{cite ODNB|last1=Moser |first1=Claus |title=Nissel [née Griffiths], Muriel (1921–2010) |url=http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/article/103069 |year=2004 |publisher=OUP |doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/103069 |isbn=978-0-19-861411-1 |access-date=26 November 2017}}</ref>

She grew up in [[Potters Bar]], Middlesex.<ref name="ONDB"/> She was educated at [[Queenswood School]], in [[Hatfield, Hertfordshire|Hatfield]], having won a boarding scholarship, followed by [[St Hugh's College, Oxford]], where she earned a first-class degree in [[philosophy, politics, and economics]] in 1942.<ref name="ONDB"/>

==Career==
After Oxford, she joined the [[Ministry of Fuel and Power]] in 1942, working as an economic statistician for [[Harold Wilson]] the future Prime Minister.<ref name="ONDB"/>

In 1964 Nissel joined the [[London School of Economics]] as a research assistant, working there with Professor [[Claus Moser]], who became her mentor.<ref name="guardian">{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2010/nov/28/muriel-nissel-obituary|title=Muriel Nissel obituary|first=Julie|last=Bindel|date=28 November 2010|work=The Guardian|access-date=26 November 2017|via=www.theguardian.com}}</ref> Later in 1964, Nissel also joined the government's [[Central Statistical Office (United Kingdom)|Central Statistical Office]] (CSO) as a financial statistician.<ref name="ONDB"/><ref name="guardian"/>

In 1967 she and Moser started work on "a national survey analysing trends in social welfare", that was to become ''[[Social Trends]]'', first published in 1970, and considered to be the "statistician's bible".<ref name="ONDB"/><ref name="guardian"/> She edited ''Social Trends'' until 1975, when she began work on the "distribution and redistribution of wealth".<ref name="guardian"/>

Nissel also wrote well-regarded books, including ''People Count &ndash; a history of the General Register Office'', and ''Married to the Amadeus: Life with a String Quartet''.<ref name="guardian"/>

==Publications==
* ''People Count: A History of the General Register Office'', HMSO, 1987. {{ISBN|0-11-691183-2}}
* ''Married to the Amadeus: Life with a String Quartet'', {{ISBN|1-900357-12-7}}, Giles de la Mare Publishers Limited

==Personal life==
On 26 January 1946, she married William Hans Barbour (1913–2000), and they later divorced.<ref name="ONDB"/> On 5 April 1957, having changed her name to Muriel Morley, she married [[Siegmund Nissel|Siegmund Walter "Sigi" Nissel]] (1922–2008), the violinist and member of the [[Amadeus Quartet]].<ref name="ONDB"/> They had two children, Claire (born 1958) and Daniel (born 1962).<ref name="ONDB"/>
